name: Oklahoma

events.title: Statehood
events.text: Oklahoma became the 46th state on November 16, 1907. Congress gave it 5 seats in the House until the next apportionment.

events.title: 1910 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1910 census, Oklahoma's House delegation grew from 5 to 8 seats.

events.title: Some members elected at-large
events.text: In the 63rd Congress (1913–1915), Oklahoma elected 3 of its representatives statewide (at-large) and the rest by district.

events.title: 1930 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1930 census, Oklahoma's House delegation grew from 8 to 9 seats.

events.title: Some members elected at-large
events.text: In the 73rd through 77th Congresses (1933–1943), Oklahoma elected one of its representatives statewide (at-large) and the rest by district.

events.title: 1940 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1940 census, Oklahoma's House delegation shrank from 9 to 8 seats.

events.title: 1950 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1950 census, Oklahoma's House delegation shrank from 8 to 6 seats.

events.title: 1960 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1960 census, Oklahoma kept 6 seats in the House.

events.title: 1970 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1970 census, Oklahoma kept 6 seats in the House. Because districts must have nearly equal populations, the map was redrawn with the new census counts.

events.title: 1980 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1980 census, Oklahoma kept 6 seats in the House. Because districts must have nearly equal populations, the map was redrawn with the new census counts.

events.title: 1990 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1990 census, Oklahoma kept 6 seats in the House. Because districts must have nearly equal populations, the map was redrawn with the new census counts.

events.title: 2000 census apportionment
events.text: After the 2000 census, Oklahoma's House delegation shrank from 6 to 5 seats. Because districts must have nearly equal populations, the map was redrawn with the new census counts.

events.title: Court adopts governor's plan after deadlock
events.text: The legislature deadlocked on a five-district plan, so a state trial court adopted the governor's proposal in May 2002. The Oklahoma Supreme Court affirmed in Alexander v. Taylor, and a federal challenge was also rejected.

events.title: 2010 census apportionment
events.text: After the 2010 census, Oklahoma kept 5 seats in the House. Because districts must have nearly equal populations, the map was redrawn with the new census counts.

events.title: Legislature redraws after 2020 census
events.text: The legislature passed a new congressional plan (HB 1002) on November 19, 2021, and the governor signed it on November 22, 2021.

events.title: 2020 census apportionment
events.text: After the 2020 census, Oklahoma kept 5 seats in the House. Because districts must have nearly equal populations, the map was redrawn with the new census counts.

compactnessNote: Polsby-Popper compactness (4π × area ÷ perimeter²) measured on the projected district shapes. It describes shape only: coastlines, rivers and county lines lower it too, so a low score is not evidence of intent. "Irregular" marks the least compact 5% of district shapes in each census era nationally.

c063.text: After the 1910 census raised Oklahoma's seats from 5 to 8, the state kept its existing districts and elected 3 members statewide (at-large).

c064.text: Oklahoma's district lines were redrawn between censuses, first used in the 1914 election. The reason has not been researched yet.

c073.text: After the 1930 census raised Oklahoma's seats from 8 to 9, the state kept its existing districts and elected one member statewide (at-large).

c078.text: No district lines moved; Oklahoma stopped electing a member at-large.

c083.text: New map drawn after the 1950 census, which cut Oklahoma's seats from 8 to 6. It was first used in the 1952 election.

c091.text: Oklahoma's district lines were redrawn between censuses, first used in the 1968 election. The reason has not been researched yet.

c093.text: New map drawn after the 1970 census, which left Oklahoma with 6 seats. It was first used in the 1972 election.

c098.text: New map drawn after the 1980 census, which left Oklahoma with 6 seats. It was first used in the 1982 election.

c103.text: New map drawn after the 1990 census, which left Oklahoma with 6 seats. It was first used in the 1992 election.

c108.text: New map following: Court adopts governor's plan after deadlock. The legislature deadlocked on a five-district plan, so a state trial court adopted the governor's proposal in May 2002. The Oklahoma Supreme Court affirmed in Alexander v. Taylor, and a federal challenge was also rejected.

c113.text: New map drawn after the 2010 census, which left Oklahoma with 5 seats. It was first used in the 2012 election.

c118.text: New map following: Legislature redraws after 2020 census. The legislature passed a new congressional plan (HB 1002) on November 19, 2021, and the governor signed it on November 22, 2021.
